blurb: Grass-like foliage sending up stalks of three-petalled violet-blue flowers with bright yellow anthers. Each flower lasts a single day and dissolves into a drop of jelly, but a clump opens a fresh set every morning for weeks.
water: Low to moderate; occasional deep soak in summer heat
spread: Clumping from fleshy roots; spreads slowly and self-sows
seasons: Three-petalled violet-blue flowers through summer, each lasting one morning; grass-like foliage dies back in winter
wildlife: Native bees and butterflies work the flowers

care.hardiness: CSU lists this as a Colorado native plantable to about 8,000 ft, so cold is not the constraint at Boulder's zone 5b–6a.[1]
care.planting: Plant in spring after the mid-May last frost, or in early fall, into ground prepared to suit it (see Soil). Set out young container plants — most of these natives resent having an established root system disturbed — and water them in well, then taper off.[1][2]
care.sun: Full sun to part shade, which is CSU's exposure rating for it.[1]
care.soil: Most soils, per CSU, though it is at its best in sandy or loamy ground with drainage. It is genuinely adaptable and one of the easier natives to place.[1]
care.water: Low to moderate. CSU rates its moisture requirement low to moderate, and on the semi-arid Front Range that is the number that matters most — the commonest way to kill a xeric native here is kindness with the hose.[1][2]
care.spacing: Space to suit its mature spread of 12–18 in wide. Upright stalks above grass-like foliage carrying clusters of three-petalled flowers, each lasting a day — CSU rates it for most soils.[1]
care.propagation: By seed, which is how nearly all of these natives are raised and how they persist in a planting. Autumn sowing outdoors lets winter provide the chilling most of them want.[1]
care.bloom: Flowers roughly June through mid-August; CSU records the colour as purple, blue and the height as 12–24 in tall.[1]
care.maintenance: Low. Cut old growth back in late winter or early spring rather than in fall, so the stems hold snow and give the crown some cover. Skip fertilizer: lean soil keeps these natives compact and long-lived.[1][2]
care.troubles: Few pests or diseases when it is sited right. Crown and root rot in soil that stays wet is the usual cause of failure for a Colorado native in a Front Range garden, and it is a siting problem rather than bad luck.[1][2]

edible.summary: No documented culinary use in the authorities consulted; grown as a native ornamental.[1]
edible.caution: No authority consulted documents a food use for prairie spiderwort, so this guide treats it as inedible — don't eat it. Spiderworts appear in some foraging accounts, but no extension or botanical-garden authority in this guide's trusted set documents it, and that is the bar used here. The sap is mucilaginous and can irritate sensitive skin.[1]
